stem: A nurse manager evaluates whether reducing registered-nurse staffing could affect patient safety. Which conclusion is most consistent with the evidence base?

options.A: Assume lower RN staffing improves safety because fewer nurses reduce handoffs and therefore consistently decrease communication-related errors.
options.B: Recognize inadequate or lower RN staffing as a patient-safety risk associated in observational evidence with missed care, adverse outcomes, and higher mortality.
options.C: Assume staffing does not influence patient outcomes when the number of occupied beds stays constant across the shift.
options.D: Treat RN staffing only as a financial issue because clinical evidence has not linked workload or staffing with patient-safety outcomes.

rationale: AHRQ PSNet summarizes evidence that appropriate nurse staffing is critical to patient safety. Fewer nurses caring for patients is associated with higher mortality; inadequate staffing can lead to missed nursing care and negative outcomes, and missed care is more prevalent with low staffing. Because much of this evidence is observational and the staffing-outcome relationship is complex, the safest wording is an association rather than an absolute causal claim. B is correct.
educational_objective: Recognize inadequate RN staffing as a patient-safety risk associated with missed nursing care and adverse patient outcomes while interpreting staffing evidence with appropriate causal caution.
source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), Patient Safety Network (PSNet)
source_document_title: Patient Safety Amid Nursing Workforce Challenges
source_locator: Introduction: appropriate nurse staffing is critical to patient safety; fewer nurses are associated with higher patient mortality. Nursing Workforce Challenges and Patient Safety: inadequate staffing can lead to missed care and negative outcomes; missed care is more prevalent with low staffing; appropriate staffing tends to reduce avoidable harm.
source_claim_supported: Lower/inadequate nurse staffing is associated with missed nursing care and adverse patient-safety outcomes, including higher mortality, although the relationship is complex and much evidence is observational.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care, printed p.7: prioritize care based on acuity; participate in quality improvement; utilize resources to promote quality care; organize workload to manage time effectively; practice and advocate for quality and cost-effective care.
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — staffing, workload, resource use and patient safety

correction_summary: Retained the staffing-safety construct and key B, strengthened causal precision by explicitly describing the evidence as associative/observational rather than deterministic, verified Management of Care on the rendered NCSBN p.7 page, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: AHRQ PSNet evidence synthesis/perspective; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.exact_locator: AHRQ Introduction and Nursing Workforce Challenges and Patient Safety; NCSBN printed p.7 rendered screenshot verified
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item preserves the direction of the evidence while avoiding an unsupported claim that staffing alone deterministically causes every adverse outcome.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect; evidence does not show lower staffing consistently improves safety.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect; staffing/workload can affect care even when occupied-bed count is unchanged.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect; staffing is linked in the evidence base to patient-safety outcomes, not merely finances.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B reflects the evidence with appropriate causal caution.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are managerial interpretations of staffing evidence; B is not keyed by length alone.
audit_findings.blueprint: Management of Care — workload, resources, quality and patient safety.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read AHRQ's wording on association, missed care and mortality, the official NCSBN p.7 screenshot, all options, rationale and objective. B remained uniquely correct and causally calibrated.
